unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Describe heat transfer by conduction, convection and radiation.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Describe matter as particles in constant motion except at absolute zero.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain that every system has thermal energy from particle motion.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Define temperature as the average kinetic energy of particles.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Relate temperature change to energy transferred through heat capacity when no state change occurs.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain changes of state through internal energy changes and latent heat.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain that systems in contact exchange energy until they reach thermal equilibrium.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain that a thermal system can do mechanical work and that doing work changes internal energy.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Apply energy conservation: internal energy change equals heating plus work done.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain why energy transformations in machines always lose heat so efficiency is below 100 percent.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Describe the nuclear model of the atom with protons, neutrons and electrons.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain nuclear stability through the strong force opposing proton repulsion.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Describe how unstable nuclides decay by emitting alpha, beta or gamma radiation.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain that each radionuclide has a characteristic half-life.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: State that alpha, beta and gamma radiation can ionise atoms.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Use mass change and Einstein's relationship to find energy released in nuclear reactions.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Distinguish spontaneous decay from artificial transmutation of nuclides.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Describe neutron-induced fission of a heavy nuclide into smaller nuclides with energy released.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain fission chain reactions, controlled for heat or uncontrolled as explosions.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Describe fusion of light nuclides into heavier ones with energy released.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain why fusion releases more energy per nucleon than fission.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain how circuits carry electrical energy over distance and convert it to heat, motion and light.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain that current is carried by discrete charges and charge is conserved everywhere in a circuit.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Apply energy conservation to transfers and transformations in a circuit.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Define potential difference as energy change per unit charge between two points.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Explain that separating charges creates a potential difference that drives current.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Define power as the rate of energy transformation in a component and use it quantitatively.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Define resistance for ohmic and non-ohmic components as potential difference divided by current.

unit: Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics
outcome: Calculate potential difference, current and power for components in series, parallel and mixed circuits.

Describe waves as periodic oscillations transferring energy.
Tell longitudinal from transverse waves by oscillation direction relative to wave velocity.
Represent waves with diagrams and relate period, amplitude, wavelength, frequency and velocity.

Use the wave model to explain reflection and refraction, such as echoes and seismic effects.
Explain superposition, standing waves and interference, including in pipes and strings.
Explain resonance when a system is driven at a natural frequency.
Explain why light shows wave properties but is not a mechanical wave since it crosses a vacuum.
Use the ray model for reflection, refraction and image formation by lenses and mirrors.
Use the wave model to explain reflection, refraction, total internal reflection, dispersion, diffraction and interference.
State that light speed is finite and enormous and its intensity falls with the inverse square of distance.

Describe the predictable motion of free-falling bodies in Earth's field.
Use Newton's law of universal gravitation to calculate attraction between masses.
Explain gravitational force through the field that masses create around them.
Explain work done on or by a gravitational field when a mass changes potential energy.
Define gravitational field strength as force per unit mass at a point.
Resolve weight into components along and perpendicular to an inclined plane.
Analyse projectile motion using independent horizontal and vertical components.
Explain uniform circular motion as a constant net force perpendicular to velocity, including banked tracks.
Use universal gravitation to explain Kepler's laws and satellite or planetary orbits.
Use Coulomb's law to calculate the force between charged objects.
Explain electrostatic force through the electric field charges create.
Define electric field strength as force per unit charge and give its direction for a positive charge.
Explain work done on or by an electric field as a charge's potential energy changes.
Describe magnetic fields around current-carrying wires and their use in solenoids and electromagnets.
Define magnetic flux density as the strength of a current's magnetic field.
Explain forces on magnets, moving charges and current-carrying wires in a magnetic field, as in DC motors.
Define magnetic flux from flux density and area.
Explain induction by changing flux and its use in transformers, generators and AC motors.
Use Lenz's law, an expression of energy conservation, to find induced current direction.
Describe electromagnetic waves as transverse waves of perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields.
Explain that oscillating charges emit waves of the same frequency and waves make charges oscillate.

Explain mass-energy equivalence as the source of nuclear reaction energy.
Explain that atomic phenomena show energy and matter in discrete quantised values.
Describe photons as light packets whose energy is proportional to frequency via Planck's constant.
Use light quanta to explain black body radiation and the photoelectric effect.

Explain that energy and matter show both wave and particle behaviour, as in double-slit interference.
Describe matter as made of quarks and leptons, with only quarks feeling the strong force.
Explain three fundamental forces through exchange of gauge bosons.
Represent particle reactions with simple reaction diagrams.
Use conservation of lepton and baryon number to test proposed reactions.
Find reaction variants using time reversal and particle-antiparticle symmetry.
Explain how high-energy accelerators test particle theories including the Standard Model.
Use the Standard Model to describe the evolution of forces and creation of matter in the Big Bang.
